p.x:
Last year, I was staying with my grandparents in a small town in the north when an earthquake happened. It was about 10 p.m. Suddenly, the house began to shake. Plates fell from the shelves, and the lights went out. My grandfather shouted, "Hide under the table!" We stayed there until the shaking stopped.
Then we escaped from the house and stood in the street with our neighbours. My grandmother brought blankets, and I used my phone as a torch. Some old buildings were damaged, and we could smell smoke from a small fire. An ambulance arrived to help two people who were injured. Luckily, nobody was missing.
The next day, we heard on the radio that there was still danger from aftershocks. A warning told people to stay away from damaged buildings. I'll never forget that night.

On 26 December 2004, a huge earthquake under the sea near Indonesia caused a tsunami that hit many countries around the Indian Ocean. In Thailand, giant waves struck the Andaman coast, including Phuket and Khao Lak. It was one of the worst natural disasters in modern history, and more than 5,000 people died in Thailand alone.
Many survivors described how the sea suddenly went out, leaving fish on the sand. Some tourists walked onto the beach to look, not knowing the danger. Others noticed animals running away and climbed to higher ground. Fishermen in boats far out at sea were surprisingly safe, because tsunami waves are small in deep water.
After the disaster, thousands of volunteers came to help, and people around the world donated money. The waves had destroyed whole villages, but many communities were rebuilt. Today, the coast has warning towers, and signs show the way to safe areas. Schools teach children how to evacuate quickly. As one survivor said, "The sea gave us a terrible lesson, but we learned it."

Natural disasters are, by definition, beyond human control. When a volcano erupts or an earthquake of high magnitude strikes, nobody can stop it. Yet the difference between a dangerous event and a devastating catastrophe often depends on human decisions.
Consider two earthquakes of similar strength. In a country with strict building codes, buildings may sway but remain standing. In a country where rules are ignored, the same tremor can cause thousands of casualties as schools and homes collapse, leaving people trapped beneath the ruins. Aftershocks can continue for weeks, making rescue efforts even harder.
For this reason, experts increasingly focus on preparedness rather than response alone. Early-warning systems, regular drills and clear evacuation routes save lives. Communities living near volcanoes, for instance, are trained to recognise the signs that lava may soon flow, and to leave quickly.
Equally important is resilience: the ability of a community to recover. After the initial relief effort, when food, water and medicine are delivered, the long work of rebuilding begins. Societies that invest in strong institutions, insurance and social networks bounce back faster. Disasters may be natural, experts argue, but their consequences are largely shaped by people.
